title: Kiddush
hookLine: a cup of wine or grape juice declares the day holy, remembering creation and the Exodus
last: YOU DON'T HAVE TO KNOW THE WORDS.

lines: A FULL CUP ON FRIDAY NIGHT.
cards: At a wedding, someone taps a glass, everyone stands, and a toast turns an ordinary evening into an occasion. Same room, same people. But now it's official: this night matters.

On Friday night, in Jewish homes, there's a moment like that at the table. Someone lifts a full cup of wine or grape juice, the room goes quiet, and the words turn a Friday evening into something else.

teach.b: Kiddush means making holy, from the same root as kadosh, holy. It comes from the commandment, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."
The rabbis asked: how do you remember a day?
You say so, out loud, over a cup of wine, the drink of celebration. Grape juice works too, and some families use it. If there's no wine at all, the blessing can be said over the challah.

On Friday night, Kiddush begins with the last lines of the creation story in Genesis: "And the heaven and the earth were finished, and all the host of them." Then God rested on the seventh day and blessed it.
Next comes the blessing over the fruit of the vine, then a longer blessing that names two reasons for the day. Shabbat is a remembrance of creation, the world God made and finished.
And it's a reminder of the Exodus, leaving Egypt. Why the Exodus? In Deuteronomy, the Sabbath commandment says: remember that you were a slave in Egypt.
Free people do. So every Friday night, one cup holds two memories: the world was made, and the slaves went free. Customs vary.

teach.h: REMEMBER THE SABBATH DAY, TO KEEP IT HOLY.
teach.b: Some hold the cup in the palm of the hand. Afterward, everyone takes a sip, often from little cups poured from the big one. It's short.
But like the toast at a wedding, it says out loud: this time is different.

how: On Friday night, before the meal, someone at the table lifts a cup of wine or grape juice and recites Kiddush, beginning with Genesis 2:1–3, and everyone then takes a sip.

o: a toast to good health at a wedding meal
making holy: a blessing over wine for Shabbat
a prayer for mourners said in synagogue

games.q: what's inside the cup — tap the pairs.
p: the heaven and the earth were finished

s: grape juice works too; without either, it can be said over bread.
Friday night Kiddush begins with the end of the creation story
"And the heaven and the earth were finished, and all the host of them."
it remembers creation and the Exodus from Egypt.

games.q: you're one of the rabbis. the Torah says remember the Sabbath day. how do you remember a day?
o: say it out loud over a cup of wine.
games.why: the rabbis read 'remember' as saying it aloud, and they set that remembering over a cup of wine: Kiddush.

practice: Pick up whatever drink is near you, water or coffee is fine, or picture one. Think of one thing in your life you didn't make but get to enjoy, and one way you're more free than you once were.
Lift the cup a little and say one sentence of thanks, out loud if you can, to God if you pray, then drink slowly.

wordCard.voice: Kiddush. Making holy: a blessing over wine or grape juice that declares Shabbat holy, remembering creation and the Exodus.

orig.note: Hebrew: making holy, from kadosh, holy.

carryVoice: Your line: make it holy out loud. You remember a day by saying so. Day one hundred two is in the books.
